ARC: Silla-Tang War (670–676)

=== EPISODE 87: Mount Gain (665)
## Bear Ford
Two springs after the river, the empire names a governor for what is left of Baekje. It is Buyeo Yung. He once knelt at Bupmin's horse and was spat on. Then he went to the emperor's city and came back in imperial robes. Now he will rule from the fortress where his father was arrested.
The court in Surabol hears the name and goes very quiet. Their men died for this ground. An emperor promised it to Chunchu by lamplight. Now a Baekje prince sits on it again, with the emperor's seal in his hand.
munmu: Everything south of Pyongyang, and the whole of Baekje. / My father made me learn it by heart.
Yung moves into the commandery offices in the spring. The rooms his father was taken from have been whitewashed. Liu Rengui shows him the registers, and the calendar, and the list of names he may not write.
liurengui: Your households, Commander. Every one of them a number now. It makes them much easier to look after.
yung: …My father counted them by name. / He was wrong about most things. Not that.
## The Altar
The next summer, the empire makes the two men who rule the south swear to be brothers. It picks a hill outside Bear Ford. The clerks name it the Mountain Where One Goes for Gain. They mean it kindly.
An imperial envoy presides. The Black Tortoise wrote the oath. On one side of the altar stands Munmu. On the other stands Yung. Munmu last saw that face at the height of his horse's knees.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 6, Silla Annals — King Munmu, yr. 5 (665), eighth month] The king, with the imperial envoy Liu Renyuan and Buyeo Yung, Commander-in-chief of Ungjin, swore a covenant on Mount Chwiri at Ungjin.
## The White Horse
An oath of this weight needs a white horse. The Tang adjutant has been walking the Silla lines all morning looking for one, and stops in front of the only white horse in the camp.
Tang adjutant: That one. Whose is he?
Hanseul is past twenty. He has carried Yushin across the Yellow Mountain. He has carried rice through snow up to his chest. His muzzle has gone grey. On a white horse, only the man who feeds him notices.
munmu: No. Find another. That is my uncle’s—
yushin: Let them have him, Majesty.
munmu: Uncle.
yushin: A white horse is what they asked for. It would be a poor oath on a brown one. / …I’ll walk him up myself.
He leads Hanseul up the hill by the halter, the way he led Hangyul across the Wolseong yard eighteen years before, talking to him in the low voice he keeps for horses and uses on no one else. At the altar he holds the head himself.
The knife is Tang. The blood goes into a bowl, and both men touch it to their lips. Yung does it without looking at anyone. Munmu does it looking at his uncle’s hands.
liurengui: …Let them be as brothers, sharing disaster and pitying each other’s sorrows, forever as one. / Whoever breaks this covenant, may the gods see it; may a hundred calamities fall on him, may his sons not grow, and may no one remain to keep his altars.
The covenant is written out three times. One copy is buried at the altar with the horse. One goes to Chang’an. The third is carried to Surabol and laid up in Silla’s ancestral temple, where the kings of Silla will have to walk past it every time they visit their fathers.
## Surabol
On the road home nobody in the Silla column says anything about the horse.
In Surabol the anger is louder. Men bled for this land in three wars. An emperor promised it to them. Now they have sworn on a dead horse never to take it. The young officers say betrayal in the barracks. The older ones say nothing. They start counting Tang garrisons.
That night the king finds his uncle in the stable, cleaning a stall that is empty.
munmu: I’ll find you another white horse, Uncle.
yushin: I’m seventy, Majesty. I’ve buried three. / Find me a war instead. I’d like to go to one more before they make me swear to something else.
To find the first king of this land, we have to go back before there were kingdoms… to a bear in a cave…!

=== EPISODE 88: Dangun & Old Joseon (Long ago) [flashback]
Before there are any kingdoms, there is a son in heaven who keeps looking down. He is Hwanung. His father Hwanin, the Lord of Heaven, notices, looks down himself at a mountain called Taebaek and the people living around it, and decides the world could use his son.
[diagram joseon-mandate]
Hwanin does not plough — he opens the sky. Three seals go down with his son, so that nobody on the ground can mistake him for a prince playing at exile. Every later king in this chronicle will cut seals of his own, and every one of them is copying these.
Hwanung lands on a mountain under the sacred birch. He names the ground beneath it the Divine City. Three thousand followers come down with him. Among them are the lords of wind, rain and cloud. Someone has to argue with the weather.
[QUOTE Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Wonder 1 — Old Joseon (Dangun); Ha & Mintz tr., pp. 32–33] He granted three heavenly seals and sent him to govern. Hwanung led a following of three thousand and descended under the sacred altar-tree on the summit of Mount Taebaek; this was called the Divine City. He married the bear-woman, and she bore a son named Dangun Wanggeom.
That is the short way to tell it, the way it is carved on stones. The long way begins, as long ways do, with a bear who wanted something so badly that she outlasted a tiger for it.
From there he hands out civilisation in instalments. Laws. Punishments. Lifespans. Illness. Good and evil. Medicine. Three hundred and sixty matters in all. Somebody counted.
A bear and a tiger come to him and ask to be made human. He gives them a bundle of mugwort, twenty cloves of garlic, and one instruction: stay out of the sun for a hundred days.
The bear stays. She comes out a woman on the twenty-first morning, garlic still on her breath, and finds the mountain already staffed — wind, rain, cloud, and not one of them a husband. So she stands under the sacred tree. Not once. Every day, on the path he has to take if he means to reach the hall.
He means to reach the hall. On the third evening he gets as far as the birch, and the seal in his hand becomes a thing he is holding for no reason he can name.
ungnyeo: You're going to walk past again.
hwanung: …Not today.
ungnyeo: Yesterday you did. / And the day before. I was standing right here.
hwanung: I saw you. / The garlic reached this far.
ungnyeo: Twenty-one days of that, and this is what came out. / …I was going to say don't come closer.
hwanung: Too late. / Stay. I mean— don't go. Your hand—
ungnyeo: You already have the hand. / …Scared of the rest?
hwanung: I am. / Because you're looking at me.
ungnyeo: Then come down. / The tree can watch. I want… more.
The kiss is clumsy. Beard, a new mouth, birch bark at her back. She makes a small furious sound and tries again, and the second one lands.
White silk goes down among the roots. The fur at her throat opens under his mouth. She laughs once, startled at the sound, and pulls him down by the hair.
By the time the moon clears the snow on the peak, the rust-red sash is somewhere in the moss, and neither of them has gone back up the path.
ungnyeo: …You're going already?
hwanung: I can't. / I don't know where I put the seal.
ungnyeo: Under my head. / I took it. …Don't go.
hwanung: …Thief.
ungnyeo: Marry me in the morning. / Right now I'm here.
Their son is Dangun. The name on the stone is Wanggeom: a king who governs, not one who inherits a bone rank. He founds Asadal where the mountain meets the plain. He rules for fifteen hundred years, and then he becomes the mountain.
Every later crown in these kingdoms argues, one way or another, back to the woman who used to be a bear.
## The Fall of Joseon
Joseon outlives its founder by a long way. Two thousand years on it is still there, run by other kings now, from a walled city on the Taedong that has kept his name: Wanggeom. In the autumn of 109 BC, Han comes to the gate.
It takes the empire of the West a year to take one fortress, and they do not take it. Wanggeom holds through a siege that begins in the autumn and is still going the following autumn.
So they stop attacking the walls and start talking to the men behind them, which is cheaper and has never once failed.
King Ugeo has stopped sleeping in the palace. He sleeps on the wall, where he can hear the Han camp coughing, and his son, Prince Jang Hang, has started sleeping somewhere else.
janghang: Father. They’ve sent terms again. / Open the gate, they say, and nobody inside gets hurt.
ugeo: They said that last autumn. / Who brought it to you?
janghang: …Does it matter who?
ugeo: It matters. / Get off my wall.
Noin, one of the ministers who have been doing the talking, goes over the wall that week and dies on the road before he reaches the Han tents. Another of them, Sam, does not bother with the road. One night at the start of summer he sends men up the wall-stair instead.
Seong Gi: Majesty—!
ugeo: …Seong Gi? / Don’t hold the city. Not for me. / Get the people out. Live… and make a new country. Anywhere.
Seong Gi closes the king’s eyes, goes back up to the parapet, and holds the city anyway.
He holds it until Noin’s son Choi and the prince go down into the lanes, where people have been eating bark since the spring.
choi: The king is dead. / So who are you starving for now? Him?
Before morning Seong Gi is dead too.
Someone lifts the bar.
herald: The wall did not come down.
herald: A door was opened from the inside.
Han takes Wanggeom. Some of the people the king told to live go south over the mountains. They settle in six villages around Surabol. Two generations later, they'll go looking for a king. The rest stay, and the empire cuts them into four pieces. The last piece is still collecting taxes four hundred years later.
Eight hundred years later, the empire comes back to the same river to do the same thing. This time, Goguryeo has a prince left…!

=== EPISODE 89: Anseung (670)
## The Protectorate
Nearly eight hundred years after Wanggeom, the empire of the West comes back to the Taedong and does the same thing again. The Third Emperor sets up a Protectorate over Goguryeo, staffs it with his own officials, and seems surprised that anyone minds.
Geom Mojam raises the old flag on the Taedong. He puts a royal cousin, Anseung, under it. Then they quarrel.
The quarrel is about whether to fight. Geom Mojam wants to hold the Taedong and die on it if he has to. Anseung has seen what the Tang do to cities that hold, and would rather be a guest somewhere than a corpse in a capital.
Geom Mojam: Pyongyang has kings in its soil four hundred years deep. You want to leave them for a Silla guest room?
Anseung: The kings in the soil will keep. The four thousand households above it won’t.
That night Anseung has him killed. It is the first Goguryeo blood the revival spills, and it is spilled by Goguryeo.
Munmu gives him a title, a district, and a name for the thing: Goguryeo, still standing, inside Silla. It is a useful fiction and both sides know exactly how useful.
Silla settles him in a town that was somebody else's kingdom ten years ago. Within the year he is called King of Goguryeo. In time he gets a bride, and a seat at Munmu's feasts. Well below the king's.
munmu: A king of Goguryeo in Silla. The emperor will hate it. / Good. Give him a seal. A big one.
Xue Rengui sends a letter. Munmu has been waiting twenty years to answer it…!

=== EPISODE 90: Letters (671)
## The First Letter
In high summer, a Tang monk is rowed ashore under a white flag. He carries a letter from the fleet. The fleet belongs to Xue Rengui, the second White Tiger. He has sat off the coast all summer. If it can be managed, he'd like to win this war by post.
Imyun: The Commander sends his respects, Majesty. He asks that it be read aloud. / He says it reads better aloud.
xuerengui: To the King of Silla, from Xue Rengui, Commander of the Eastern Fleet, greetings. / A clear wind blows ten thousand li from the capital to your coast, and the sea between is three thousand. I have come all of it to say one thing. / Your father knelt before the Second Emperor and was raised up. He was given robes, and a brother, and an army. You were given his crown. / And now you take the land the emperor’s soldiers bled for, and you shelter his rebels, and your own brother waits in Chang’an, ashamed to be asked about you. / Turn back while there is still a road to turn on. / I have the honour to remain, in all things but this, Your Majesty’s servant — / Xue Rengui.
The monk is given a bed, a meal, and as long as it takes. The king does not go to bed at all.
## The Writing Room
By the second night the king’s writing room is full of men with opinions. One of them, an official named Daeto, has more than most.
daeto: Majesty, a softer word here and there costs nothing. / They have a fleet off Bear Ford. They have Prince Inmun. Could we not say we were mistaken about the border? Everyone is mistaken about borders.
munmu: We were not mistaken. / Write it the way I say it.
There is another reason the room is careful. Nine summers ago, the king killed a great lord and his whole house for calling in sick. The lord's son wasn't in the house. He's in the emperor's guard. Somebody there will have told him by now.
## The Reply
munmu: To the Commander of the Eastern Fleet, from the King of Silla. / Your letter came by a monk, and was read aloud as you asked. It does read better aloud. So will this.
He dictates the rest standing up, and does not stop for most of the night.
munmu: In the twenty-second year of Zhenguan my father went to Chang’an. The Second Emperor took him into a gallery of stone horses and said: everything south of Pyongyang, and the whole of Baekje, shall be Silla’s, forever. / My father made me learn those words when I was twenty-two. I have them still. I expect the emperor’s clerks have them too.
munmu: When your Red Fowl sat outside Pyongyang eating his horses, my uncle was sixty-seven. He walked beside his own white horse through snow to its chest so the horse could carry rice instead of him. Your soldiers wept when they saw the carts. Your general took the rice and sailed home the same week. / We were late, he said. We are always late. We came anyway.
munmu: Then you gave Baekje back to a Baekje prince, with a Tang seal, at Bear Ford. Then you took us up a hill called Gain and made us swear to be his brother over a dead horse. / The horse was my uncle’s. He walked it up himself. I watched his hands.
munmu: At Pyongyang our men went through the gate first. Then your Protectorate came and wrote our share down as nothing. / You say I shelter rebels. I shelter the people your officials could not be bothered to count.
munmu: My brother is in Chang’an. Tell him I am well. Tell him I said his name. / I have the honour to remain the king of the country you came to save — / Bupmin.
Daeto copies it out fair. His hand is very steady. Later that night he writes a second letter, a short one, to a different address, and puts it in his sleeve, and does not send it yet.
## The Second Letter
xuerengui: Your Majesty’s letter has been received, and read aloud. It took most of an afternoon. / Nowhere in it is the word “sorry.” / I have the honour to remain your servant, in fewer things than before — / Xue.
munmu: The Commander’s letter has been received. It took no time at all. / Nowhere in it is the word “rice.” / I have the honour to remain the king — / B.
xuerengui: Then I will come and fetch the apology myself. / — X.
munmu: Come, then. / — B.
## Seventy Ships
He comes. In the tenth month, off the western coast, a Silla squadron finds seventy Tang transports riding low with grain for the garrison at Bear Ford, and takes them: hulls, crews, one Tang colonel, and all of the rice.
munmu: Send word to the White Tiger that his rice has arrived. / Late. As usual.
The Tang are coming south. Silla is winning. That is exactly when armies start to chase…!

=== EPISODE 91: Stone Gate (672)
## Stone Gate
The Tang take Hansi and Mapeup and come south. Silla and what is left of the Goguryeo revival meet them, cut down several thousand, and then make the mistake that costs the year: they chase.
At Seokmun the Tang turn around. The Mohe cavalry come in on a Silla army that has not yet formed up, and it is over in an afternoon.
Silla sends an apology to Chang’an and hands back the prisoners. Then it goes quiet, and starts building.
[FLASHBACK 659 A room in Surabol, a year before Baekje falls]
  chunchu: Bupmin. What do you think happens after Baekje falls?
  munmu: We move on Goryeo.
  chunchu: And after that.
  munmu: …Unification.
  chunchu: No. / After that, it is our turn.
  He lays it out the way another man would lay out a field. The Tang will not go home. They will put a governor in Sabi and call it a commandery. They will give you a title with the word province in it and expect you to be flattered. They will keep your brother in Chang’an and call him a guest.
  chunchu: When it comes, never strike first. / Wait until they have exhausted themselves in the north. / Take the fortresses back one at a time, and send an apology after each one. / What they want is not the land. It is the paperwork.
  munmu: …And the sea?
  chunchu: The sea is last. / After they have lost the horses.
  munmu: Father. How do you know all of this?
  chunchu: Li Shimin taught me. / I wrote down everything he intended to do to me.
One lieutenant came home from Stone Gate alive. His father is Kim Yushin…!

=== EPISODE 92: Wonsul (672)
Wonsul, Yushin’s second son, is told to die there and does not. He comes home. His father will not see him, and his mother will not either, and he spends the rest of his life trying to give the afternoon back.
yushin: He shamed the king’s command and the family name with it. He is not my son.
The retreat is almost beside the point. Wonsul ran and lived; a hundred men did the same that afternoon and kept their fathers. But a house that arrived in Silla by treaty rather than by birth does not get to be ordinary — it has to be exemplary, permanently, in every generation, or it is simply Gaya again.
yushin: Another man’s son may retreat. / Mine may not.
Yushin goes to the king and asks, in so many words, for his son to be put to death. It is the most formal request he has made in fifty years of service, and he makes it standing.
munmu: Uncle. He was a lieutenant. Lieutenants follow. / If I execute every man who lived through Seokmun, I won’t have an army left to lose the next one with.
yushin: Then do not execute him, Majesty. / But do not ask me to call him back into my house.
Wonsul does not go home. He goes into the hill farms east of the capital and works another man’s fields under no name at all, which is the one punishment his father did not think to ask for. He does not write. Twice he comes as far as the road below his father’s gate and turns back at the sight of the lamp.
Farmer: You hold a hoe like it owes you money. / Soldier, were you?
Wonsul: No. / …Not a good one.
Yushin is old now. The three sisters in the steam are not. They have kept his ledge warm for fifty years…!

=== EPISODE 93: Kim Yushin† (673)
## THE LAKE REMEMBERS
Old now, between campaigns that are mostly paperwork, Yushin still finds the cavern. The steam is thinner. The three are not. They look the same age they always looked — which is either mercy or mockery, and he has never asked which.
Hyullé’s hand finds the water beside the ledge where he always sits, and stays there. Fifty years of the same ledge.
narim: You still undress like a soldier checking for wounds. / Sit. The counsel is shorter these days. So is the war. Slower. Let me look at you.
golhwa: He’s going to say it. / Watch — three, two —
yushin: But Her Majesty is gone. / …I still hear myself saying it.
golhwa: Ugh… even in the Western Flower Field she gets the title. / What did that mortal have that we don’t? / …Don’t answer. Stay until the steam drops. Before the hill keeps you.
hyulle: I didn’t — bring — / …It’s just warmer there. / You always liked it. Come sit. Please.
The steam thins. For a breath his father’s mouth is in the water — not the counsel, only the name — and then it is steam again.
He sits. For once he does not rush the border. Narim talks about a tree that outlived three kings. Golhwa falls asleep against the stone mid-complaint. Hyullé says nothing, and that is the visit he will remember when the biographies start lying.
Seventh month, 673. He is seventy-nine. He has fought for sixty of those years and outlived nearly everyone worth outliving.
The King comes to the house himself, which kings do not do. Munmu does it anyway — he has known this man his entire life, and for most of it has not been sure whether to call him Marshal or uncle.
munmu: Yushin…
yushin: Princess…
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 43, Biographies — Kim Yushin (final counsel); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2, p. 404] I humbly pray Your Highness know that to succeed is not easy, and to keep what has been won is also hard. Keep petty men far and good men near.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 43, Biographies — Kim Yushin (Munmu’s lament); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2, p. 406] That I have you is as a fish having water.
Kangrim reads his name three times at the bedside — Yushin. Yushin. Yushin. — before the marshal's last answer.
kangrim: Marshal. / One hundred and eight draws, one win that ended a friend, sixty years of being useful. / Question: were you becoming Silla — or proving you never needed their blood to outserve them?
yushin: …I wanted in. / Wanting in is not shameful. Pretending I did not is.
kangrim: Clean answer. / His Majesty’s kingdom has room for men who told the truth late.
Munhee is in the courtyard when they come out. She is sixty-seven. Once she was the girl in the burnt-skirt rumour. She has been a queen, then a queen mother. Her sister has been in the ground for years. After tonight, she is the last of three children from a house that used to be a country.
munhee: Brother. Are you a Silla man now?
yushin: …I don’t know. Ask them for me.
He is buried at Geumsan with the honours of a king and the rank of a subject. Somebody will close that gap. It takes a hundred and sixty years.
The same month, an official named Daeto is found to have been writing to the Tang, promising them a door, the way a man at Daeya once promised Baekje a granary. He is executed, his wife and children are made slaves, and nobody mentions it at the funeral.
— Kim Yushin —
His grandfather bought the family a rank with a kingdom. That was the deal: Gaya for True Bone, one generation for the next. Everyone honoured it. Everyone also remembered it, which was the part the deal did not cover.
So he became necessary instead. Forty fortresses. The Hwarang. The one name that opened a prison door in Pyongyang. If you cannot be one of them by blood you can be the thing they cannot do without, and he was very, very good at being that.
He married his sister into the royal house and called it strategy. He married a princess himself, late, and called that strategy too. He loved a queen for forty years and never once said so where it could be heard. Assimilation is a long word for wanting to be let in.
The taunt came in the end from the boy who had given him a headband. You were never even of Silla. Sixty years of service and it was still available, still sharp, still the first thing an enemy reached for.
He outlived the queen, the friend, the war and most of the men he trained. They gave him a posthumous title no subject had ever held. It is the most Silla thing imaginable: they would not let him in while he was alive, and once he was safely dead they made him a king.
## Lady Jiso
After the funeral Wonsul comes down from the hills at last and asks at the gate for his mother. Lady Jiso is King Muyeol’s daughter and Yushin’s widow, and she has already cut her hair for the nunnery.
Lady Jiso: A woman has three to follow. Her father, her husband, her son. / My husband would not call you son. How am I to be your mother?
She does not come to the gate. The answer is carried out by a servant who cannot look at him. Wonsul stands in the road until dark and then goes back up into the hills. The record says only that he left weeping, and that he never stopped trying to give the afternoon back.
His uncle never showed him the path. Munmu finds it anyway, and something older than any kingdom is waiting on the water…!

=== EPISODE 94: The Wanggeom's Guest (673)
After the funeral rites, Munmu rides alone into the hills east of Surabol. Yushin never showed him the path; he found it anyway, the way sons find what uncles hid on purpose.
He takes the best of both — the uncle’s steam, which no record kept, and the first king’s name, which every stone still does. The lake has not yet named the stranger on the water.
He strips at the rock lip as if obeying an order nobody ever gave him in writing, and steps into water so black it reflects nothing.
Crimson leaves his shoulders the way a soldier sheds a campaign coat. Steam takes the rest. He does not look up until the water has him.
They smell him before they see him — uncle’s heat, father’s road-dust, both houses in one walk. He still thinks he is alone. Time drops. Golhwa’s mouth opens and does not close. Hyullé cannot get a word out. Narim bites her lip and fails at being eldest.
He is the best of both — they said it first when he was twenty-one and the jar was still cold, and they say it again now that the uncle is ash. Gaya in the shoulders. Surabol in the mouth. A Kim they have not had as king. Fire comes off Golhwa’s skin. Water streams from Hyullé’s chin. A leaf turns in the steam around Narim and will not fall.
munmu: Who… / Who lives here. I was looking for a spring my uncle named.
narim: We do. You fell. / The door is the name. Kim. You came the same way. Sit—
He looks at her like she is kind. Narim cannot finish the sentence. Out of breath, and she pretends the steam did that. Sit down before I ask you to put me on the rock, she does not say. Fuck. Uncle’s shoulders. Father’s mouth. She is not supposed to want both.
golhwa: Oh. Oh no. / He’s both. Hi. I’m Golhwa. That’s unnie. That’s Hyullé. Don’t look at me like that or I am going to say the stupid thing.
golhwa: The stupid thing is I want to sit on you.
golhwa: You’re both— / I can’t sit. I haven’t even said hello properly.
Gaya shoulders. Surabol mouth. She has been on the rock since the uncle left. She wants him to pin her until she goes insane.
hyulle: Hello. I’ll be quiet.
hyulle: I’m already wet. Please ignore both.
Silk on Hyullé is only water now. She stands near him and looks like she will explode. The hello is all she can get out. In the steam she is already filled. She will not say it. He keeps the black water as a wall. He does not climb out.
narim: Sit down before you fall in again. / We are the mouths the hill uses. Wisdom, if you stand in the water and ask once. The uncle is gone. The hill is not.
munmu: I came because he died. / …Will the west stay taken.
The comedy goes out of the cave. When they speak again the eyes are solid — green, cyan, ember.
narim: The west will take your name and call it peace. / Keep a sea in the other hand.
golhwa: That was the hill. This is me. / Come back anyway. You’re both. I can’t sit. I want you back in the water with nothing on, and that is the stupid thing.
Then the steam goes thin enough to see through, and a man stands on the water as if the lake were a court floor — old robes, sandalwood-coloured light, a face that has outlived every kingdom on the map. The three go still on the rock. This visitor is not theirs.
dangun: You wanted a king for all when you were six. / The title you are looking for is older than your father’s reforms. / Wanggeom — not Sacred Bone, not True Bone. The first who stayed when heaven descended.
munmu: Who are you. / Which court sent you.
dangun: Asadal is dust. / The mandate is not. / Finish what your uncle could not name aloud.
Munmu tells no one. The court records note only a day’s ride and a night’s silence. The chronicle knows because the steam keeps Kim heirs, and because later, when he expels the Tang and takes the title King of Samhan, someone in Surabol remembers the word wanggeom and does not explain it.
Kim Punghun said he could wait for a ship. The ship is here…!

=== EPISODE 95: Maeso (675)
## The Landing
Xue Rengui comes back by sea in the ninth month. His pilot is Kim Punghun. Munmu killed his father. Now the son is showing the enemy fleet the way into his own coast.
He is older now. The white coat is a reputation he can no longer take off. Tang’s eastern command sits on his shoulders the way a yoke sits on an ox that still believes in the field.
xuerengui: Silla… the country that once fought beside us. / And now that country is to be my last opponent.
He does not curse them. He checks the ji’s bindings, the same way he once checked plough-rope, and goes ashore.
Above the beach at Cheonseong, a Silla general named Munhun lies flat in the dune grass and watches the boats come in. He has been told to stop the landing. He has decided to let it happen first.
Silla captain: General, they’re unloading the horses. Horses first.
Munhun: Good. Let them.
Silla captain: We were told to stop the landing.
Munhun: We will. / A horse on wet sand can’t turn. Wait till the boats are empty.
When the last horse is off, Munhun stands up.
xuerengui: To the boats.
By evening Munhun has fourteen hundred heads, forty Tang ships, and a thousand horses standing in the surf with nobody to ride them. The sea road is closed again.
## Maeso Fortress
So the war moves inland, to a fortress on the Imjin where the road to Surabol begins.
The army at Maeso is mostly Mohe, and the Mohe are mostly horse. Thirty thousand of them graze the flats under the walls. The grass is outside. No fortress on that river was built to stable a herd.
Silla commander: Forget the walls. / Cut the picket lines. Bring me the horses.
Before dawn the herd moves all at once, and not toward the fortress.
Mohe rider: The horses! The horses are going!
Horses are the thing. An army that has lost thirty thousand horses on the Imjin is not riding to Surabol next spring, or the spring after.
One of the men who cut the picket lines that night is a lieutenant nobody in the capital has seen for three years. Wonsul comes down out of the hills when he hears where the Tang have gone, asks for the worst stretch of the line, and leads the horse-cut himself. When the king sends for him afterwards to give him rank, he will not take it. He says the rank belongs to the afternoon at Seokmun, and he has not paid that off yet.
Out at sea off Cheonseong, Xue hears it from a courier: the army at Maeso has lost its horses.
xuerengui: …So the horses are gone. / For a farmer, losing horses… is like losing the field.
He withdraws without spectacle. The chronicle will remember Silla’s thirty thousand horses; it will remember less how quietly the White Tiger II accepted that the east was no longer his to harvest.
In Surabol the number arrives a day ahead of the generals.
Messenger: Thirty thousand, three hundred and eighty, Majesty.
munmu: …Heads?
Messenger: Horses, Majesty.
After they have lost the horses. Munmu is nearly fifty and still, occasionally, checking his father’s work against the day.
munmu: Then get me ships. / It’s the sea now.
One last river mouth. One middling captain. Three tries to end a war…!

=== EPISODE 96: Final Ford (676)
In the second month, the emperor's headquarters quietly leaves Pyongyang. Then it moves further. Then nobody mentions it. Xue still has a fleet, and a fleet doesn't need a headquarters.
The last of it happens at the mouth of the Geum, in the eleventh month, in water Seongchung had begged a different king to hold twenty years earlier.
The Silla ships belong to a sachan named Sideuk, a middling rank for a man about to be handed the end of a war. He takes them out on the ebb and loses.
Silla helmsman: Sachan, we’re going out again?
Sideuk: When the tide turns.
He goes out again and loses again.
Silla helmsman: …And a third time?
Sideuk: Their ships are big. / A big ship can’t turn on the mudflats. Draw them in.
The third time he does not try to win. He runs, up the estuary and over the mudflats, and the Tang fleet comes in after him. What follows is twenty-two fights, large and small, in water too shallow for the ships that started them.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 7, Silla Annals — King Munmu, yr. 16 (676), 11th month, Gibeolpo; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 168] Sachan Sideuk led ship-troops and fought Xue Rengui at Gibeolpo in Soburi-ju; they were defeated. They advanced again, fought twenty-two engagements great and small, prevailed, and took more than four thousand heads.
No treaty comes after it, and no envoy. The war simply stops being fought, and the first anyone in Surabol hears of it is a messenger with river mud still on his feet.
Messenger: Majesty. At Gibeolpo… the Tang ships are pulling out. / They’re heading west. None of them are turning back.
munmu: Have we… won…?
The boy who stole a sentence at six is about to be king of all Samhan. His mother would like him to hold still…!

=== EPISODE 97: The King for All (676)
Bupmin, King Munmu now, stands where a six-year-old once stole a sentence. The war is won, the ally has been shown the door, and the childhood dream has had the bad manners to come true.
munmu: Mother. / I kept the childhood sentence.
munhee: I know. / I packed for every country that tried to stop you.
It ends where it began: a woman in a room, getting someone else ready.
Munhee is seventy. She is the last person alive who remembers all of it from the inside, and she is straightening her son's collar. She was twenty-six when this story started. Her sister burned a skirt on a hill so that she could be married.
munhee: Hold still. Your collar is crooked.
munmu: Mother. Today I become king of all Samhan.
munhee: Then all the more reason to hold still.
She has been in the room for every single one of them. The wedding she was not supposed to have. The daughter who did not come home from Daeya. The husband who came back from the West with a name nobody else was allowed to say. The brother who was never quite let in. She was never the one holding the sword and she is the only one still standing.
munmu: Father used to say a thing. A kingdom that lasts a thousand years.
munhee: He always did round the numbers up.
Silla lasts nine hundred and ninety-two years. He was, as usual, very slightly optimistic and essentially correct.
## 681
Five summers later the king for all is dying, and he has left instructions his ministers do not like. No mound in the hills beside his fathers. Burn him, and put what is left in the sea the Wa come across.
[QUOTE Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 2, Wonder 2 — King Munmu becomes a dragon; Ha & Mintz tr., p. 95] After I am gone I wish to become a great dragon that guards the country, to uphold the Buddha’s law and protect the realm.
They burn him on the shore and put his bones under a rock a hundred paces out to sea, which is still there, and is the only royal tomb in the world with tides.
## 692
Eleven years after the tide closes over him, an envoy comes from the Empress’s court with a complaint that is thirty years late. King Muyeol’s tablet in Silla’s ancestral temple says Taejong, and Taejong is the Second Emperor’s temple name, and a vassal may not share a name with the Son of Heaven.
Tang envoy: Your late king has borrowed a name that belongs to the Second Emperor. / Change it.
Munmu’s son answers in writing.
Silla reply: Our late king had a great deal of virtue. While he lived he had a good minister, Kim Yushin, and the two of them were of one mind, and they made the three Han one. / We thought that was worth a name. We did not know it was already taken.
The court reads the name Kim Yushin, and somebody there remembers a story about him, and the complaint is dropped. The tablet still says Taejong.
But we left someone in the snow. The winter Pyongyang fell, a Mohe father walked north with something in his pack…!
